questions.title: How does 1.58 bits arise from ternary weights {−1, 0, 1}?
questions.question_body: The paper claims each weight is in {−1, 0, 1} and calls the model "1.58-bit". I assume this is because there are 3 states and log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits. Is this just a naming convention (information-theoretic) or does the implementation actually use packed encodings close to 1.58 bits/weight at runtime? If the kernel uses 2-bit packing (as mentioned via Ladder), then the effective storage is 2 bits/weight, not 1.58. Can the authors clarify what is 1.58 vs 2 bits in practice (storage on disk, in-memory, wire, and compute representation)?

questions.title: Where does the scaling factor go after absmean quantization of weights?
questions.question_body: The quantization is defined as \(\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma+\epsilon), -1, 1)\) with \(\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij} |W_{ij}|\). After rounding, are the ternary weights used as-is (\{-1,0,1\}) or is there an implicit multiplication by \(\gamma\) somewhere (e.g., folding \(\gamma\) into activations or a layerwise scaling)? If \(\gamma\) is thrown away, how is dynamic range preserved? If it is kept, where is it applied at inference so that matrix multiplies remain multiplication-free?

questions.title: How are gradients computed through the RoundClip operator during training?
questions.question_body: The paper says BitNet b1.58 is trained from scratch with 1.58-bit weights, implying quantization is present throughout training. What surrogate gradient is used for \(\mathrm{round}(\cdot)\) and clipping (e.g., straight-through estimator with clip-aware gradient)? Is there any gradient scaling by \(\gamma\)? Also, is \(\gamma\) treated as a constant per weight matrix (frozen per step) or differentiated through?

questions.title: What exactly is meant by “no multiplication operations” in matrix multiplication?
questions.question_body: With weights in \{-1,0,1\}, a dot product with 8-bit activations can be implemented as additions and sign flips (and skips for zeros). But the paper also mentions using a 2-bit kernel from Ladder. Does the actual kernel use any multiplications (e.g., bit-serial popcount tricks or table lookups) or is it strictly addition/subtraction and shift? Can you detail the primitive operations used per MAC and how that translates to the claimed energy savings?

questions.title: Are all Transformer parameters ternary, or are some layers left in higher precision?
questions.question_body: The paper says "every parameter (or weight) of the LLM is ternary" but elsewhere notes that the embedding "remains full precision" in scaling analyses. Which components are ternary versus higher precision at inference: token embeddings, positional/rotary embedding parameters, attention projection matrices (Q/K/V/O), MLP (SwiGLU) matrices, layer norm/RMSNorm parameters, and output softmax head? If some remain FP16/BF16, how does that affect the reported memory and speed numbers?

questions.title: Why are biases removed, and how does that interact with ternary constraints?
questions.question_body: The model removes all biases and uses RMSNorm and SwiGLU (LLaMA-like). Is bias removal primarily for numerical stability/quantization compatibility, for simplicity, or to match LLaMA configs? In ternary networks, biases can help shift activation distributions. Did keeping biases degrade training stability or performance here, or was removal just for reproducibility with LLaMA?

questions.title: Clarifying activation quantization: per-token scaling to [−Q_b, Q_b] without zero-point
questions.question_body: The paper states activations are 8-bit and scaled per token to \([-Q_b, Q_b]\), removing zero-point. 1) How is the per-token scale determined (max-abs, EMA, percentile)? 2) Is scaling applied before or after attention softmax, and how is numerical stability ensured for attention scores and softmax? 3) Does per-token scaling break any invariances or cause sequence-position-dependent artifacts compared to per-channel or per-tensor schemes? 4) Why was the previous BitNet activation scaling to \([0, Q_b]\) dropped—did it hurt performance or complicate kernels?

questions.title: How does the inclusion of 0 in ternary weights improve “feature filtering”?
questions.question_body: The paper claims adding the 0 state explicitly improves modeling by enabling feature filtering. Is there empirical evidence at the weight or activation level (e.g., sparsity patterns) showing that a significant fraction of weights or effective connections become zero? Does the training encourage structured sparsity (e.g., at channel or block level), and is there any regularization that promotes the 0 state?

questions.title: Reconciling 2-bit kernels with ternary weights: how are codes mapped?
questions.question_body: Since weights are in \{-1,0,1\}, a 2-bit code can represent 3 values plus one unused. Which code mapping is used, and does the kernel exploit the unused code for any optimization (e.g., run-lengths or block sparsity)? Also, does the kernel handle mixed signed activations, or are activations also recoded for faster addition?

questions.title: What evaluation settings were used for latency per output token?
questions.question_body: The paper reports time per output token using FasterTransformer. Could you specify the full inference configuration: batch size(s), context length, use of KV cache, attention implementation, GPU model and clock settings, tensor parallelism, and whether pinned memory/async prefetch was used? Since time/token depends heavily on these, a detailed setup would help reproduce the reported 2.4–4.1× speedups.

questions.title: How was memory usage measured and what remains in full precision?
questions.question_body: For the reported 3.3–3.6× memory reductions, what is included: model weights, optimizer states (for training?), KV cache, activation buffers, and temporary workspace? Given embeddings may remain FP16 and KV caches are 8-bit per the paper, can you provide a per-component memory breakdown for a representative model (e.g., 7B) at a given batch size and sequence length?

questions.title: Energy model assumptions behind the 71.4× arithmetic savings
questions.question_body: Figure references claim 71.4× energy savings in matrix multiplication arithmetic on 7nm. Which per-operation energy costs were assumed for FP16 multiply/add versus INT8 add? Are memory access energies included or only ALU operations? If the latter, how does the end-to-end energy claim incorporate memory and control overheads? A concrete equation or table with the constants used would clarify the derivation.

questions.title: Why does BitNet b1.58 match FP16 perplexity only from 3B and up?
questions.question_body: Results suggest parity begins at around 3B parameters. Is there a known capacity or expressivity threshold for ternary-weight Transformers that causes underperformance at smaller scales? Did you attempt architectural tweaks (e.g., wider MLPs, more heads) at smaller sizes to recover performance, or is the gap mostly due to quantization noise being amortized at scale?

questions.title: What is meant by a “new scaling law” for 1.58-bit LLMs?
questions.question_body: The paper states BitNet b1.58 defines a new scaling law relating model performance and inference cost. Is this an empirical Pareto frontier (accuracy vs latency/memory/energy) or a formal relation akin to Chinchilla/compute-optimal laws (loss vs parameters vs tokens)? If formal, can you state the functional form and data used to fit it? If empirical, can you share the curve and methodology for the model-size equivalences (13B b1.58 ≈ 3B FP16, etc.)?

questions.title: Throughput results on two A100s: what parallelism and KV-cache sharding were used?
questions.question_body: For the 70B throughput experiment on two 80GB A100 GPUs, you mention pipeline parallelism. Were tensor-parallel or sequence-parallel techniques also used? How was the KV cache partitioned across devices? Since b1.58 supports much larger batch sizes, is the 8.9× throughput gain limited by interconnect bandwidth, kernel launch overheads, or compute? More details would help understand bottlenecks.

questions.title: How is rotary embedding handled with 8-bit activations and ternary weights?
questions.question_body: Rotary positional embeddings are multiplicative/rotational transforms on Q/K. Given 8-bit activations and ternary weights, are rotary operations performed in higher precision (e.g., FP16) before re-quantization, or directly in INT8? If done in FP16, does this materially affect the claim of near-multiplication-free compute? What precision is used for attention score computation and softmax?

questions.title: KV cache quantization: how do you maintain accuracy with 8-bit (and proposed 4-bit) caches?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that reducing activations from 16 to 8 bits allows doubling context length, and even "lossless" compression to 4 bits for 1.58-bit LLMs is suggested as future work. 1) How are K and V cached quantization scales selected and updated across time steps? 2) What error control ensures negligible degradation at long contexts? 3) On what basis is 4-bit "lossless" considered feasible—do you rely on constrained dynamic ranges from ternary weights, and is there empirical evidence?

questions.title: How do SwiGLU activations behave under per-token 8-bit scaling?
questions.question_body: SwiGLU involves elementwise products and nonlinearity. With per-token 8-bit quantization, how do you prevent saturation or information loss at the gates? Are intermediate products computed in higher precision and then requantized? Any calibration or learned scale parameters per channel to stabilize training/inference?

questions.title: Training from scratch with 1.58-bit weights: what optimizer and schedules were stable?
questions.question_body: Quantized-from-scratch training can be unstable. What optimizer (AdamW?), weight decay, learning rate schedule, warmup, and regularization were used to reach parity at 100B and 2T tokens? Any special tricks (e.g., gradient clipping thresholds, loss scaling, EMA of weights before quantization, knowledge distillation, or auxiliary losses) needed specifically for the ternary setting?

questions.title: Fairness of comparisons: are tokenizers, data deduplication, and evaluation prompts identical?
questions.question_body: For the FP16 LLaMA-like baseline vs b1.58, were tokenizers identical, training data deduplication and filtering identical, and evaluation prompt templates exactly the same (e.g., lm-evaluation-harness settings)? Small differences can shift zero-shot accuracies, so a detailed comparison protocol would help interpret the reported parity and improvements.

questions.title: Does ternary quantization encourage structured sparsity that kernels can exploit?
questions.question_body: With \{−1, 0, 1\} weights, zeros may appear frequently. Do your trained models exhibit significant block or channel-level sparsity that could be exploited by sparse kernels to further reduce compute/memory bandwidth? If so, what sparsity patterns and densities are observed across layers and model sizes?

questions.title: What are the implications for MoE routing and communication with 1.58-bit weights?
questions.question_body: The paper argues MoE becomes more deployable due to reduced memory and activation transfer costs. In a concrete MoE setup (e.g., top-2 gating with N experts), how would you quantize and transmit activations and expert weights? Are gating logits/dispatch indices also quantized, and does quantization affect load balancing or expert specialization?

questions.title: Storage vs compute precision: what precision is used on disk, in RAM, and in the kernel?
questions.question_body: To deploy b1.58, models might be stored in compressed formats on disk, unpacked into GPU memory, and then processed by specialized kernels. Could you specify the precisions at each stage (disk, host RAM, device global memory, shared memory/registers) and the associated bandwidth/compression strategies? This would clarify practical gains vs theoretical 1.58 bits/weight.

questions.title: How does adding the 0 state compare to scaled binary weights (±α) in practice?
questions.question_body: Some 1-bit methods use binary weights with a learned or estimated per-channel/per-tensor scale \(\alpha\) to recover dynamic range. Your approach uses ternary \{-1,0,1\} with an absmean normalization. Did you compare against binary-with-scale baselines of similar complexity? Where does ternary help most (e.g., attention vs MLP), and is the gain mainly from induced sparsity or better approximation of small-magnitude weights?

questions.title: Do residual connections accumulate quantization error, and how is it controlled?
questions.question_body: In Transformers, residual connections can amplify quantization noise across layers. With 8-bit activations and ternary weights, do you observe drift or instability in deep stacks? Are there normalization tweaks (e.g., post-norm RMSNorm parameters in higher precision) or periodic rescaling to keep residual streams within safe dynamic ranges?

questions.title: Is there any calibration or post-training fine-tuning after from-scratch quantized training?
questions.question_body: After training from scratch with 1.58-bit weights, did you run any short calibration or post-finetuning pass (e.g., collecting activation ranges, adjusting per-layer scales, or distillation on a held-out set) to improve final inference performance? If not, would such a step further narrow any remaining gaps at sub-3B scales?
